name: Wax kit

lead: A wax kit is a set of supplies for waxing, with warm wax or pre-made cold strips plus applicators. It removes body hair at the root for smooth skin that lasts longer than shaving, and is also used to shape brows and clean up the face.

Wax grips the hair and removes it from the follicle when pulled away, so regrowth takes about three to six weeks and tends to be softer than after shaving. Hair-removal reviews classify waxing as a temporary epilation method. No clinical trials of consumer wax kits were identified.

paras: Users apply wax in the direction of hair growth and pull strips against it, working in small sections, then soothe the skin afterward. Home kits cover legs, arms and brows, and salons offer the same service. Sessions repeat every few weeks.

Burns from overheated wax, skin lifting, folliculitis and ingrown hairs are the main risks. Waxing is advised against on irritated, sunburnt or broken skin, and skin lifting is more likely with certain skin conditions or medications.

angle.text: Users wax body hair, and sometimes brows or the face, at home for smoothness that lasts weeks and to shape brow lines. Hair is pulled from the follicle, so regrowth takes longer than after shaving. Skin irritation is a recognized downside.

lead: A wax kit is a set of supplies for waxing, a method of hair removal in which a sticky substance is applied to the skin, adheres to the hair, and is pulled away to remove the hair from the follicle.[1] People use it to get smooth skin on the chest, back, arms, legs, brows and other areas for weeks at a time, which is longer than shaving gives, and the result is often described as a cleaner, more defined look.[1][2] Home kits typically include warm wax or pre-made cold strips, applicators or spatulas, and cloth or paper strips; waxing is also offered professionally in salons.[1][3]

Because hairs are removed at the root rather than cut at the surface, regrowth is described as taking about four to six weeks, although some people see regrowth sooner because individual hairs are at different stages of the growth cycle [1]. Hair removal reviews classify waxing and sugaring as epilation methods and list them among the temporary approaches to hair removal [4].

Common concerns include pain, ingrown hairs, folliculitis, burns from overheated wax and 'skin lifting', in which the top layer of skin is torn away, which is more likely in people with certain skin conditions or medications [1][3]. No clinical trials of consumer wax kits were identified.

paras: Wikipedia distinguishes strip waxing from stripless waxing. In strip waxing, a soft wax is spread thinly in the direction of hair growth, a cloth or paper strip is pressed on, and the strip is pulled off against the direction of growth, ideally parallel to the skin. Strip waxes may be heated, cold or supplied as pre-made strips already coated with wax [1].

Stripless waxes include hard wax and film wax. They are applied more thickly (hard wax) or as a thin film, harden as they cool and are lifted off without a strip. Wikipedia reports that stripless waxing adheres less to the skin than strip waxing and is sometimes described as better suited to sensitive skin and finer hairs [1].

According to Grokipedia, wax mixtures generally combine natural or synthetic resins for grip with oils or waxes such as beeswax for spreadability and emulsifiers for stability, and hair is said to need to be roughly a quarter to three-quarters of an inch long for effective waxing [3].

Hair removal has been practised in nearly every human culture since at least the Neolithic era, using flint, shells, beeswax and abrasive or caustic substances.[2] In ancient Egypt it was a fashion among the wealthy and a response to lice, priests removed body hair for ritual purity, and Greece and Rome used depilatory preparations and attendants who removed bathers' hair.[2] Smooth skin in Rome signalled purity and rank.[2]

Modern routines took shape later: the first safety razor for men appeared in 1760, and hair removal became a regular part of women's personal care in the late nineteenth century, helped by a 1915 Harper's Bazaar promotion of underarm hair removal and Gillette's first razor marketed to women.[2] Wikipedia describes waxing as a form of epilation, alongside sugaring and threading, and contrasts it with shaving, a depilation method that lasts only hours to days.[2]

The wax mechanically grips the hair shaft. When the wax or strip is pulled away, the hair is extracted along with its root from the follicle, so a new hair has to regrow from below the skin [1]. Grokipedia describes the effect as strongest on hairs in the active growth (anagen) phase, which are firmly anchored [3]. Wikipedia adds that areas waxed repeatedly over long periods often show softer regrowth [1].

Wikipedia gives hair-free periods of two to eight weeks, noting that shaving or depilatory cream leaves stubble within days because the hair is removed at the surface rather than the root [1]. Grokipedia states results last three to six weeks and that some users report finer hair over time [3].

A 2021 literature review states that all hair removal methods other than electrolysis are temporary, and that most studies of effectiveness are limited to darker hair and fairer skin [4]. A 2019 review of hirsutism in women similarly lists shaving, waxing and plucking as effective but temporary, with photoepilation and electrolysis described as somewhat effective for long-term removal but expensive [5].

Wikipedia lists factors that make skin lifting more likely: blood-thinning medication, drugs for autoimmune disease, prednisone or other steroids, psoriasis, eczema or other chronic skin conditions, recent sunburn, recent cosmetic or reconstructive surgery or laser treatment, severe varicose veins, rosacea or very sensitive skin, a history of cold sores, use of topical retinoids such as tretinoin, tazarotene or adapalene, and recent chemical peels or acid-based exfoliation [1]. Grokipedia likewise says waxing is not recommended on sensitive, sunburned or recently medicated skin, and mentions burns when wax is overheated [3].

Pain, redness, swelling, ingrown hairs, red bumps, minor bleeding and folliculitis are the effects most often listed, and ingrown hairs are said to be more likely on thick hair and in the first sessions [1][3]. A 2023 review of hair removal in the genital area discusses skin reactions and infection risks associated with waxing and other methods in that region [6].
Wikipedia also notes that do-it-yourself supplies can be hard to use on some body areas, and that professional waxing carries a cost that varies with the area and number of sessions [1].

Reference sources describe hair removal as widespread: most Western women shave legs and underarms, and most Western and Asian men shave facial hair regularly, with male body grooming ('manscaping') growing.[2] Professional footballers and road cyclists remove leg hair so injuries are easier to clean and treat and massages are more comfortable, and competitive swimmers shave to reduce drag.[2]
Waxing is available both in salons and as consumer kits sold in warm-wax and pre-made strip formats.[1]

The word manscaping, a blend of man and landscaping, is first recorded in 2003, and Cambridge Dictionary defines it as removing or cutting a man's body hair to improve his appearance.[7] Men's grooming spending has grown globally, and Wikipedia cites East Asian markets such as South Korea and China as large and expanding.[7]

Almost any area can be waxed, including eyebrows, face, legs, arms, back, abdomen, chest, knuckles and feet.[1] For looks, brow waxing is used to define shape, while chest, abdomen and back waxing are used to present a cleaner torso. Kits sold for the face typically use smaller applicators and finer wax, and hard wax is described as suiting sensitive skin and finer hairs.[1]

Wikipedia dates the popularity of pubic hair styling partly to the introduction of the bikini in 1946, and credits the J Sisters salon in Manhattan, founded in 1987 by seven sisters from Brazil, with first offering what was called the Brazilian wax.[8] The article lists American, French and Brazilian styles, which remove progressively more hair, and notes male waxing has become more common.[8]

A 2016 JAMA Dermatology study of 3,316 American women, as summarised on Wikipedia, found 84% had groomed pubic hair at some point, with hygiene the most frequent reason given.[8] The same article reports that pain can be greater during pregnancy, that folliculitis and ingrown hairs occur, that people with weakened immune systems face infection risk, and that critics have objected to the Brazilian style on social grounds.[8] A 2023 review covers skin reactions and infection risks of genital hair removal methods.[6]

Hair removal reviews divide methods into depilation, which removes the shaft at the surface (shaving, chemical creams), and epilation, which removes the hair with its follicle or bulb (plucking, threading, waxing, sugaring, lasers, intense pulsed light, electrolysis).[4] Wikipedia describes shaving results as lasting hours to days, versus weeks for waxing.[2] Laser and electrolysis are described as longer-lasting but more expensive, and electrolysis is the only method the 2021 review lists as permanent.[4][5] The same review notes eflornithine cream is approved in the US and Canada to slow facial hair growth alongside other methods.[4]

In grooming discussions, waxing is mentioned for the chest, back, arms, legs and brows as a way to get a smoother surface that lasts longer than shaving, using either a salon or a home kit.[1] Smooth skin lets muscle definition read more clearly in photos and at the beach, which is the usual appearance reason given by people who wax the torso; athletes in sports such as swimming, cycling and wrestling have trimmed or removed body hair since antiquity for performance reasons.[7]

Wikipedia notes that do-it-yourself supplies can be hard to use on some body areas, which is one reason people book salons for the back or other hard-to-reach places.[1] A thread on the Straight Dope message board compared bikini waxing with epilator use among people who had tried both, and T Nation, a strength-training forum, mentions waxing mainly in passing.[9]
No studies found on consumer wax kits specifically. Related literature consists of general reviews of hair removal practices, which describe waxing as a temporary epilation method [4][5].

lore.intro: Waxing appears in grooming discussions as a longer-lasting alternative to shaving, with debate about pain and skin reactions.[9]
